name: System design
routing_text: Designing large scale distributed systems: database sharding and partitioning, caching strategies and invalidation, replication, consistency and availability tradeoffs, transactions and isolation levels, distributed message queues, REST API design, latency, throughput and capacity estimation in a system design interview.
blurb: Distributed-systems decisions and the tradeoffs the speakers refuse to skip.

units.title: database, sharding, shard, cache, caching, partitioning
units.summary: Caching increases read throughput by hitting memory instead of disk. For system design interviews, the most common and impactful CDN use case is media delivery. The most popular feature on hello.com is guided. Every time a queue is created, information about it is stored in the database.

units.title: microservices, module, modules, monolith, modularity, component
units.summary: A good monolith is a monolith that is easy to change, easy to modify, and easy to extend. Slices of functionality ensure exactly one request going in and one response coming out, with all logic in a single action class. Using microservices can make a system easier while the performance gets worse. Microservices are supposed to be independently deployable, unlike modules in a monolith, which are all deployed together in a single monolithic deployment.

units.title: transaction, acknowledgement, consistency, snapshot isolation, leader, load balancer
units.summary: When you ask a peer to update something, you are effectively a client for that peer. Joe Hellerstein suggested that the C in ACID was basically tossed in by the authors to make the acronym work and that they did not attach much importance to it. Serializable snapshot isolation detects serialization conflicts and aborts transactions. At low effort, GLM 52 is used with Oracle.

units.title: unity catalog, models, LLMOps, MLOps, Databricks, mlflow
units.summary: Unification around Lakehouse monitoring and Unity Catalog becomes increasingly important. A custom model can be pulled from Unity Catalog, someone else in the organization, Hugging Face Hub, or Databricks Marketplace. The SQL function AI query is optimized for batch use cases. A monitor solution can be implemented by deploying a Databricks Lakehouse monitor to the entire assets.

units.title: coupling, codebase, system, cohesion, intrusive coupling, distance
units.summary: Structured design was introduced in the 1960s and proposed six coupling levels: content, common, external, control, stamp, and data coupling. Coupling was introduced in the late 1960s, and connascence in the 1990s, creating a 30-year cadence. Architecture rules are often turned off after breaking the build because they are annoying. Integrating with a legacy system by going directly to its database is intrusive coupling.

rubrics.criterion: Keep every replicated or shared piece of data synchronized through a single source of truth or an explicit synchronization mechanism.
rubrics.check: Find each entity stored in more than one place or modified by more than one module. Fail the design if independent local copies can be written with no sync path, or if two modules modify the same business entity without sharing the same database.
rubrics.why: Unsynchronized copies put the system in an incorrect state; multiple copies are only valid if their content matches.
rubrics.unit_title: database, sharding, shard, cache, caching, partitioning

rubrics.criterion: Hide each database behind a dedicated service that owns all calls to it.
rubrics.check: Review the architecture diagram for database access paths. Every read or write to a database must pass through a dedicated web service facade; fail if frontends, clients, load balancers, or arbitrary services connect directly to the database.
rubrics.why: The creators state this as a required best practice; without the facade, components bypass the service that should handle database calls.
rubrics.unit_title: database, sharding, shard, cache, caching, partitioning

rubrics.criterion: Lock down production access to AI assets (data, models, notebooks) while keeping development environments open.
rubrics.check: In the MLOps/LLMOps architecture, compare access-control rules per environment. Production must require authorization to touch the model or data and development must allow broad access; fail if prod is open to everyone or has the same access as dev.
rubrics.why: Trust in data and model quality grows from dev to prod; an open prod lets anyone mess with the model or data.
rubrics.unit_title: database, sharding, shard, cache, caching, partitioning

rubrics.criterion: Every mutable business entity must have one owning component and one canonical database; components that modify the same entity must share that store rather than keep local copies.
rubrics.check: For each business entity, list the components that create or update it. Pass if one component owns the entity and all writes go to one canonical database. Fail if two components keep unsynchronized local copies, or if separate services share a database to access the same tables.
rubrics.why: Separate services sharing a database destroy the benefits of the service split, while unsynchronized local copies leave the system in an incorrect state.

rubrics.criterion: Do not replace a monolith with microservices just because the monolith is messy; first build explicit module boundaries and a clear dependency structure.
rubrics.check: When a microservice migration is proposed, inspect whether the monolith already has named modules, declared dependency rules, and a module-level dependency diagram before the split. If the rationale is only that the monolith is a mess and no module boundary plan exists, fail.
rubrics.why: Decomposing an already tangled monolith without modular boundaries recreates the same mess, so teams cycle from monolith to microservices and back.
rubrics.unit_title: microservices, module, modules, monolith, modularity, component

rubrics.criterion: A feature change must touch code only inside the module that owns that feature; modular boundaries must make unrelated modules safe from change.
rubrics.check: Take any single feature change and inspect its diff. All modified files must lie in one module or in that module's public interface. Fail if the diff also edits other modules, or if the regression checklist includes unrelated modules just to make sure nothing broke.
rubrics.why: When most change effort goes into not breaking anything else, coupling is working against the design rather than for it.
rubrics.unit_title: microservices, module, modules, monolith, modularity, component

rubrics.criterion: State the functional requirements, non-functional priorities, and target scale before selecting any distributed-system mechanism.
rubrics.check: Look for a written section listing functional requirements, non-functional priorities, and the scale the design must handle before any sharding, caching, or consistency strategy is chosen; if the design skips these and jumps to a mechanism, fail.
rubrics.why: Without these answers the design is guessing: the same trade-off can be right or wrong depending on requirements and scale.
rubrics.unit_title: transaction, acknowledgement, consistency, snapshot isolation, leader, load balancer

rubrics.criterion: Define module or service boundaries by the capability they own and the coupling they have, not by code size or the label 'micro'.
rubrics.check: For each service or module boundary, find a stated capability or coupling rationale; fail if the only justification is that the component is small, 'micro', or a certain number of lines of code.
rubrics.why: Sizing-based decomposition produces thousands of unmanageable services and misses the real problem of defining what belongs inside each boundary.
rubrics.unit_title: transaction, acknowledgement, consistency, snapshot isolation, leader, load balancer

rubrics.criterion: Replace bare 'ACID' or 'consistent' labels with a concrete specification of which copies must match, under what isolation, and after which durability event.
rubrics.check: For every consistency or durability claim, look for an operational definition: which replicas must agree, which isolation level applies, and what write is considered durable; fail if the design stops at the words ACID or consistent.
rubrics.why: ACID is a mnemonic rather than a precise guarantee, and consistency means different things in CAP versus ACID, so the design must say concretely what is promised.
rubrics.unit_title: transaction, acknowledgement, consistency, snapshot isolation, leader, load balancer

rubrics.criterion: Extract duplicate code into a shared helper only after the same logic has appeared three times.
rubrics.check: For each shared class or module created during decomposition, count the duplicated occurrences of that logic in the original code; fail if the shared abstraction exists before three independent occurrences.
rubrics.why: A shared abstraction created too early codifies a boundary that hasn't been proven; waiting until the third copy shows the dependency is real.

rubrics.criterion: Pick a shard key from the dominant query access pattern and state the trade-offs of that choice.
rubrics.check: Look at the sharding design: it should name the main access pattern, derive the shard key from it, and list at least one trade-off such as expensive global queries plus a mitigation; fail if the key is chosen without access-pattern analysis or trade-offs are omitted.
rubrics.why: A shard key that does not match how data is actually queried makes common reads scan many shards and aggregate results.
rubrics.unit_title: unity catalog, models, LLMOps, MLOps, Databricks, mlflow

rubrics.criterion: Isolate each concurrent agent thread in its own work tree or checkout before it edits a shared codebase.
rubrics.check: In an agentic coding system, if two threads can run against the same repository simultaneously, verify that each thread has a separate work tree or checkout, or that changes are serialized; fail if they share a single working tree and can both make changes.
rubrics.why: Without isolation, concurrent agent edits collide in the same working tree and corrupt each other's changes.
rubrics.unit_title: unity catalog, models, LLMOps, MLOps, Databricks, mlflow

rubrics.criterion: Group code for each feature set in one vertical module instead of splitting it across technical layers.
rubrics.check: For each feature set, find all its web, business, and data code and check that it lives in one package or module; fail any feature whose code is scattered across packages named by technical layer.
rubrics.why: Without boundaries around functional areas, features compete for the same code and every change forces developers to hunt down everywhere it could break.

rubrics.criterion: Judge a module's independence by counting dependencies, not by its size.
rubrics.check: For each module, count how many other modules it depends on and how many depend on it; reject designs whose boundary rationale is smallness rather than reducing those arrows.
rubrics.why: Focusing on making boxes small distributes coupled piles of code; the useful heuristic is reducing direct dependencies between modules.
rubrics.unit_title: coupling, codebase, system, cohesion, intrusive coupling, distance
